item.title: Create Music Group Buys A Minority Stake In DistroKid
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Create Music Group bought a minority stake in DistroKid, joining CVC as an investor in the independent music distributor.
item.content:encoded:
Create Music Group bought a minority stake in DistroKid, adding the label and music technology company to the distributor’s investors.

Create CEO and co-founder Jonathan Strauss confirmed the investment to Music Business Worldwide on October 28. The company invested earlier in 2026 alongside CVC Capital Partners’ majority deal, which closed in the third quarter. The reports did not disclose Create’s ownership percentage or what it paid.

“We’re excited to partner with CVC as a minority investor in the company and to support its continued growth,” Strauss said in a statement to Billboard, which also confirmed the investment.

CVC announced its agreement in July through its CVC Capital Partners IX fund. Its announcement said longtime DistroKid investor Insight Partners would keep a significant minority holding and Phil Bauer would remain president with the existing leadership team. CVC did not disclose financial terms.

Founded in 2013, DistroKid built its business around independent musicians. CVC’s announcement described a service that had expanded beyond sending music to platforms. Its tools also included video distribution, instant mastering, direct contact with fans and custom merchandise.

DistroKid also faced a separate dispute over the music it delivered. AllHipHop previously reported that the company removed recordings in response to Universal Music Group’s copyright claims. DistroKid disputed UMG’s allegations and said it was working to limit the disruption for affected artists.

Create’s own business already extended across music distribution, rights management, accounting and marketing. On its website, the company described support for artists, managers and independent labels, as well as founders building music businesses.

The investment joined Create’s broader push to buy and back music businesses. In March, Los Angeles-based Create announced a fundraising round of more than $450 million that combined equity and debt and valued the company at $2.2 billion. Create said it had put more than $500 million into acquisitions, advances and other growth efforts over the previous year.

Those investments included $300 million for Canadian independent Nettwerk Music Group to help its managers buy out existing investors. Create had also bought electronic labels Monstercat, !K7 and Cr2, plus deadmau5’s publishing and master recording catalogs. Its businesses included distribution platform Label Engine and marketing agency Flighthouse.

item.title: Cardi B Rejects Therapy After Fan Asks If She Is Getting Help
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Cardi B told a fan she had stopped seeing a therapist, a change from her earlier comments about getting help with work pressure.
item.content:encoded:
Cardi B told a fan she had no interest in returning to therapy as she vented about people close to her during an Instagram Live.

A viewer asked whether she was seeing a therapist during the October 27 broadcast, prompting a blunt answer about her recent absence from sessions.

“I haven’t seen a therapist in a minute. I don’t want to see a therapist. I want these motherfuckers to die,” she said.

She did not identify anyone in that exchange, which followed her discussion of feeling let down by people she knew personally.

Her answer marked a change from earlier public comments about getting help, including a 2024 account of finding a therapist she liked.

In that Rolling Stone interview, Cardi said she had previously struggled to focus during sessions before deciding to try counseling again.

At the time, she said trying to channel anger or sadness into recording could leave her voice cracking and make melodies harder to sing.

“So I just got a therapist, and I really like her,” Cardi told Rolling Stone.

Reporter Mankaprr Conteh described the therapist calling to check on Cardi during their time together in New York, where she was recording music.

During that interview, Cardi also described trouble finding enough help with her children while she tried to keep up with studio work.

She said the demands at home had become hers to resolve, explaining that an assistant, husband or record label could not solve them.

That same spring, Cardi shared one practical step she had taken on her therapist’s advice when she began learning to drive.

During an April 11, 2024 Instagram Live, she said her counselor wanted her to spend an hour each day on a healthy habit.

She explained that the advice came because work was consuming so much of her life, and she livestreamed her first driving lesson.

She took that lesson in a Rolls-Royce after misplacing her Bentley keys, then asked the instructor to take over when she struggled with reversing.

Near the end of the October 27 livestream, Cardi said she needed to do squats because trying to sleep would leave her thinking about the situation.

She closed the broadcast after discussing exercise, bringing the conversation back to squats before signing off from the livestream.

item.title: FortyCal Sues Pigeons & Planes Owner Over Waka Flocka & EsDeeKid Clips
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: FortyCal sued the owner of Pigeons & Planes, claiming it used his Waka Flocka Flame, EsDeeKid and Fakemink clips without permission.
item.content:encoded:
FortyCal took the owner of Pigeons & Planes to court over four concert videos, claiming the platform used his footage without paying for permission.

The Cincinnati photographer and videographer, known legally as Calan Beasley, sued Commerce Media Holdings, LLC in California federal court on October 27.

Working as Forty Cal Productions, he accused the company of using clips featuring Waka Flocka Flame, EsDeeKid and Fakemink without permission. The artists appeared in the clips, but the complaint named Commerce Media Holdings as its only defendant.

Two videos featured Waka Flocka at the 2025 Gathering of the Juggalos in Thornville, Ohio. One showed the rapper with FortyCal and fans, while the other captured him in a mosh pit.

FortyCal said he posted EsDeeKid performing “Rottweiler” at Chicago’s Avondale Music Hall on February 3, 2026. His Fakemink video captured “LV Sandals” at the artist’s first New York City show and was posted on September 8, 2025, the suit said.

According to the complaint, Pigeons & Planes accounts posted the EsDeeKid clip the next day across Facebook, Instagram, X and TikTok. The filing also identified posts using the Waka Flocka footage in August 2025 and the Fakemink clip that September.

FortyCal said he licenses his work to media companies and other businesses, arguing that unauthorized copies cost him paid licensing opportunities.

“Defendant’s use of the Videos harmed the actual market for the Videos,” the complaint stated.

He also accused the company of gaining traffic, ad revenue and promotional value from the posts. His claims included direct copyright infringement and a second claim alleging that the company controlled the people posting the clips and benefited from their use.

The U.S. Copyright Office says an original work gains protection as soon as it is recorded. Registering a work can also affect what a creator may recover through a successful lawsuit in court.

Rod Wave also faced a photographer’s copyright lawsuit over a concert photo allegedly used for his album art without permission.

FortyCal sought damages tied to his losses and the company’s profits, plus an order stopping further infringement. He sought statutory damages as an alternative only for the EsDeeKid clip, without naming a fixed dollar demand.

FortyCal also asked for a jury to hear the case against Commerce Media Holdings in federal court.

item.title: Tiffany Pollard Clash Has Philip Regan Threatening To Quit “Big Brother”
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Tiffany Pollard left Philip Regan talking about going home after their "Big Brother" clash turned into personal insults.
item.content:encoded:
Tiffany Pollard left Philip Regan talking about going home after a “Big Brother” argument on her guest return turned personal.

According to the Daily Mail, the celebrity guest called him a “huge backstabber,” describing what she said was the public’s view. She then mocked his hair loss as he headed to the Diary Room.

“I do really want go home now,” Regan said. He called Pollard nasty and later confronted her about hurting his feelings. She later compared his look to an out-of-work Steven Seagal as their dispute continued outside the Diary Room.

The report also described a separate mix-up: housemate Twinks wrongly said Angie Bowie had died. Producers corrected that claim.

Pollard had promised trouble before her guest stay. She previously shared the celebrity house with Angie Bowie in 2016, when she finished fourth.

That earlier season included a very different misunderstanding. Angie told Pollard that David had died, referring to her former husband, David Bowie. Pollard believed she meant fellow housemate David Gest.

Other contestants checked on Gest and found him asleep. Actor John Partridge then explained which David Angie had meant. Pollard had accused Angie of making a cruel joke before the confusion was cleared up.

ITV News reported in January 2016 that Ofcom had received more than 200 complaints. Viewers objected to showing Angie’s grief, Pollard’s reaction and how other housemates treated her.

The sharp exchanges also carried a history beyond that house. Pollard built her “New York” name on “Flavor Of Love” before leading “I Love New York.” Flavor Flav gave her the nickname, as a 2023 Bustle profile recalled.

But she rejected the idea that the person on screen was wholly separate from her private life. She said she sometimes forgot a camera was running and could upset people close to her, too.

Pollard also spoke about the pressure to keep giving viewers the version they first met. At 41, she said fans still wanted her to behave as she had at 23. She wanted room to choose her own response.

She said she could still confront someone when needed, while no longer seeking anger and frustration simply to help ratings.

item.title: Stevie Wonder’s Ex Alleges Manipulation
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Stevie Wonder's former fiancee Carmen Efferson accused him of breaking a home ownership promise amid their eviction dispute.
item.content:encoded:
Stevie Wonder‘s former fiancee Carmen Efferson accused him of breaking a promise to give her the home at the center of their eviction fight.

She called him a “gaslighter and a manipulator” in a Daily Mail interview reported by The Blast. Efferson said she paid for major repairs despite owing no rent and challenged his image as a community benefactor. Her account put repair bills at hundreds of thousands of dollars, including work after the 1994 Northridge earthquake and flooding. She claimed gift-tax concerns delayed a promised deed transfer.

Wonder’s charity work has included House Full of Toys, an annual benefit for children, struggling families and people with disabilities. AllHipHop previously reported that he canceled four planned December 2025 shows at Hollywood’s Fonda Theatre because there was too little time to prepare.

He addressed that cancellation on KJLH, his Los Angeles radio station, and pledged to donate money himself. The concerts would have marked the fundraiser’s 26th year. At the time, he also said he intended to bring the event back the following year.

The Blast also cited someone close to Wonder who told the Mail that safety for Efferson and neighbors drove the dispute.

The singer sued Efferson in Los Angeles Superior Court on October 22, according to documents obtained by USA TODAY. Its report described a three-bedroom Hollywood Hills house she has occupied since 1988 under what the complaint called an oral, rent-free arrangement.

The filing put access to the house at the center of the case. It accused Efferson of blocking an inspection needed to maintain insurance. Wonder’s lawyers said the home had been uninsured since August 4.

Emails described in USA TODAY’s reporting showed the standoff had escalated in July. Efferson said she felt harassed and withheld consent for anyone to enter. Attorney David Huff warned that Wonder had directed his lawyers to begin eviction proceedings if access remained blocked.

She received notice to leave by August 27 but stayed, according to the filing. Wonder asked the court to remove her and sought $600 in damages for what his lawyers called “malicious and obstructive behavior in preventing the lawful protection of the Property.”

item.title: Omari Hardwick’s “Bosch” Prequel Sets January Premiere
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Omari Hardwick plays a veteran cop who trains young Harry Bosch as MGM+ sets a January premiere for its new crime prequel.
item.content:encoded:
Omari Hardwick is putting on a badge. MGM+ shared photos from “Bosch: Start of Watch,” with a January 10, 2027 premiere, JoBlo reported.

Hardwick plays veteran Eli Bridges opposite Cameron Monaghan’s rookie Harry Bosch. Set in 1992 Los Angeles, the eight-episode season follows patrol work, a heist and police corruption. Two episodes arrive at launch, followed by weekly releases through February 21.

The role puts Hardwick on the other side of the law from James “Ghost” St. Patrick. AllHipHop covered his casting in “Power” in 2013, when he landed the lead in the Starz drama. Ghost owned a nightclub and ran a drug business while trying to go straight. 50 Cent was an executive producer and Courtney Kemp Agboh created the series and served as its showrunner.

Hardwick later spent time in jail to study the life his character faced in season four. In a 2017 appearance on “Live! with Kelly and Ryan,” covered by AllHipHop, he said he stayed for two or three nights with help from a producer and a warden. He described hearing prisoners at night while he was writing and working on an album. Hardwick said he felt more open as an artist that season than at any earlier point in his 14 years of acting.

The “Bosch” role brings him into a TV franchise built around Michael Connelly’s books. Titus Welliver played the detective for seven seasons of the original show and three seasons of “Bosch: Legacy.” Readers first met Harry Bosch in Connelly’s 1992 novel The Black Echo, long before this look at his early police work.

Connelly, an executive producer on the prequel, told Kirkus that the project gave him a chance to explore a stretch of the character’s life that had never appeared in a book. That meant writing new material for Bosch rather than adapting an existing novel.

The setting also has a personal connection for the author. Connelly worked as a reporter in Los Angeles during that period. He described 1992 as a year remembered for injustice and rebellion, while good deeds faded from view. In his telling, young Bosch would see a city the author had once covered himself.

item.title: DMC Of Run-DMC Fame Involved In Los Angeles Freeway Crash
item.dc:creator: Houston Williams
item.description: DMC’s management confirmed to AllHipHop that the Run-DMC legend was involved in a Los Angeles freeway accident.
item.content:encoded:
Darryl “DMC” McDaniels was involved in a freeway accident in Los Angeles, his management confirmed to AllHipHop. His representative said everyone involved is OK.

The founding member of Run-DMC was seen standing and speaking with fire department personnel in video obtained by AllHipHop. The footage came from a person livestreaming from the roadside following the reported collision with a garbage truck near Interstate 105 and South Hoover Street.

“Yes he’s okay, they got into a accident on the freeway but everyone is okay,” a representative for DMC told AllHipHop.

An observer also said it did not appear that anyone was seriously hurt. Authorities have not provided additional details about the circumstances or cause of the crash.

McDaniels helped establish Run-DMC alongside Joseph “Rev. Run” Simmons and the late Jason “Jam Master Jay” Mizell, becoming one of the most influential groups in Hip-Hop history.

item.title: Halle Berry Defeats Ex-Husband’s Restraining Order Request
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Halle Berry defeated Olivier Martinez's restraining-order request; custody terms stayed in place until another hearing.
item.content:encoded:
Halle Berry defeated ex-husband Olivier Martinez’s restraining-order request in Los Angeles on Thursday, October 29, according to Page Six.

Judge Shelley Kaufman dissolved the temporary order and denied his domestic violence restraining-order request involving their son, Maceo.

Berry denied abuse allegations. Her attorney, Marina Beck, told the outlet, “We are extremely pleased that the Court has dissolved the TRO.” Beck said Berry would keep her focus on her family’s best interests as the case moved forward.

Martinez’s attorney did not immediately respond to Page Six.

The fight followed years of negotiations over how the former couple would raise their son after their marriage ended. They married in July 2013 and split in October 2015. The pair became legally single in 2016, but their finances and custody terms were still unresolved.

A settlement in August 2023 addressed both issues, according to court documents obtained by Us Weekly. Their agreement gave both parents legal and physical custody, with time during the week and alternating weekends.

Berry was ordered to send Martinez $8,000 a month in child support. The terms also called for an extra 4.3 percent of income she earned above $2 million. She was responsible for their son’s tuition, extracurricular costs and health insurance as well.

By May 2024, the parents had agreed to bring in help for their co-parenting disputes. Another filing reviewed by Us Weekly outlined a coaching plan with a psychiatrist who worked with adults and children.

The plan called for each parent to meet with the doctor separately before attending at least six joint sessions. Those shared appointments were to take place by June 14, 2024. If the sessions helped, the pair could continue together for up to a year.

The doctor would set the sessions’ format, length and frequency. Van Hunt, Berry’s partner, was allowed to take part under the agreement.

Berry also has a daughter, Nahla, with former partner Gabriel Aubry. AllHipHop previously covered a reduction in the child support she paid Aubry, a separate arrangement involving her daughter’s father.

The custody arrangement under the temporary order remained in effect pending another hearing, Page Six reported.

item.title: DOJ Says FBI, ICE Won’t Be Poll Monitors
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: The Justice Department said FBI and ICE employees would not monitor polls, while other federal staff would work under limits.
item.content:encoded:
The Justice Department said FBI and Immigration and Customs Enforcement employees would not serve as poll monitors in the midterms, according to Law&Crime. Other federal agencies would still supply staff.

Eric Neff outlined the limits in an October 28 declaration. He is acting chief of the Civil Rights Division’s Voting Section. Spectrum News reported that volunteers included employees of the Federal Bureau of Prisons, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and the Drug Enforcement Administration.

One Customs and Border Protection employee would also participate, but would not represent the Department of Homeland Security, Neff said. Monitors must introduce themselves to election officials when they arrive and carry federal credentials to show if asked.

Any conversation with voters would have to wait until they finished voting and stepped outside. Neff said monitors would be unarmed and barred from law enforcement work. The assignment called for observation and notes, with business casual dress and no visible agency insignia, Law&Crime reported.

The declaration followed a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit from the NAACP against the division and its leader, Harmeet Dhillon. The group sought details about the planned 1,000 monitors, including their roles, qualifications and destinations. The NAACP argued that the expanded federal presence could undermine voters’ ability to take part without intimidation, Law&Crime reported.

Neff also argued that releasing locations could put monitors at risk because other groups planned to watch them, Law&Crime reported.

The monitoring program predates this election. An October 2024 Justice Department guide described staff visits to assess compliance with voting rights laws, including the Voting Rights Act of 1965 and the Help America Vote Act. It also distinguished those staff assignments from federal observers appointed under court orders. Attorneys and other staff could maintain contact with state and local election officials. The guide covered both federal elections and other races.

The NAACP has clashed with the administration over civil rights before. In 2025, the group excluded Donald Trump from its national convention, as AllHipHop reported.

Election Day is Tuesday, November 3. As of October 28, Neff said some monitoring locations still had to be chosen, Spectrum reported.

item.title: Vince Staples Explains The Bills Behind Touring
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Vince Staples explained why artists pay touring bills up front and how he approached his responsibilities to his live band.
item.content:encoded:
Vince Staples said touring meant paying bills before fans ever reached the room.

Speaking with Rolling Stone at New York’s Cherry Lane Theatre, he listed transportation, advance wages, insurance and venue costs. A tour couldn’t earn without ticket sales.

“Nobody’s doing that if they don’t like to do it,” he said.

He also said being his bandmates’ boss came with obligations. Road life also meant ensuring employees felt heard and were treated well, he said. Two musicians hired through open auditions had never performed live.

Staples said television work taught him to manage music projects more efficiently.

He had several jobs on “The Vince Staples Show.” Netflix credited him as a co-creator and executive producer as well as its star. The satirical comedy drew from his life and cast him as a version of himself. Its second season arrived on November 6, 2025.

The business had its limits there, too. AllHipHop reported Netflix’s cancellation of the series in January. Season 2 drew 1.7 million views through the end of 2025. The first season reached 4.6 million over a longer stretch, from February 15 through June 30, 2024.

His current live run centers on Cry Baby, released in June as his first album for Loma Vista. The “Cry Baby Tour” was announced with a live band and a route through the United States and Canada, including a Toronto stop on November 4.

Staples has also tied record sales directly to getting fans into those rooms. His official website advertised a deal with independent record stores: Buy the blue vinyl edition of Cry Baby in a participating shop and receive two tickets to the local show while supplies last.

His site named Rough Trade for Brooklyn, Soundgarden for Silver Spring and Main St. Records for Philadelphia. The offer also covered shows in Houston, Dallas, Toronto, Detroit, Denver and San Francisco. It paired a physical copy of the album with admission for two.

The next scheduled show was October 29 at The Fillmore Silver Spring in Maryland. The ticket listing put the start at 8 P.M., with all ages admitted. Later dates included Denver on November 11 and Phoenix on November 13, before the announced November 15 finale at San Francisco’s Warfield.
